name: Homologous rib cartilage graft

lead: A homologous (donor) rib cartilage graft uses cartilage from a human donor's rib, usually sterilised by gamma irradiation, as building material in the nose. Surgeons use it in revision rhinoplasty and saddle-nose repair when the patient has too little septal or ear cartilage, to rebuild the bridge and support the tip.

The benefit for appearance is a straighter, more projecting or better-supported nose without taking a second graft from the patient's own ribs. Published case series from the 1980s onward report generally stable results, while surgeons note that a patient's own cartilage is usually preferred when available.

paras: The graft is carved and shaped by the surgeon during open rhinoplasty and placed along the dorsum, tip or columella, sometimes combined with an implant. Patients do not harvest anything from themselves, which avoids a chest incision. Recovery follows standard rhinoplasty timelines under the surgeon's guidance.

Reported risks include infection, graft warping or resorption, visible contour irregularities and the need for revision. Because the cartilage comes from a donor, tissue processing and disease-transmission questions are handled through tissue-bank screening. It is major surgery that should only be done by a qualified surgeon.

The nose gains structural support, height or projection
angle.text: The graft supplies firm structural material for rebuilding the nasal bridge and tip when the patient's own cartilage is limited. It is used to correct saddle-nose deformities and revision rhinoplasty results, changing the shape and projection of the nose.

lead: Homologous rib cartilage grafting is a nasal surgery technique in which cartilage taken from a human donor's rib, commonly sterilised with gamma irradiation, is carved into pieces to rebuild or support the nose. It is also called an irradiated rib cartilage graft or an irradiated costal cartilage homograft [1][2].

Plastic surgeons use it mainly in cases where the patient's own cartilage is limited, such as revision rhinoplasty, saddle-nose deformity or after an extruded implant. For appearance, the graft restores bridge height, tip projection and structural support, which changes the nose's profile and symmetry [1][3]. Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article notes that donor rib cartilage is sometimes used when a patient's own cartilage is unsuitable [4].

Research consists largely of surgical case series. Reports from the 1980s found stable grafts with no immune response, and later series report high satisfaction with low complication rates, though most are small and uncontrolled [5][6][3].

paras: Costal cartilage is the hyaline cartilage bar that extends each rib toward the breastbone, and it can be harvested for reconstructive use elsewhere in the body [7]. Cartilage from the patient's own septum is the usual graft source in rhinoplasty; when there is not enough, surgeons turn to ear or rib cartilage, and donor rib cartilage is sometimes used [4]. Donor tissue is processed by a tissue bank and often irradiated for sterilisation, which can spare the patient a second surgical site [2].

Published reports describe the graft in saddle-nose reconstruction, where articulated irradiated rib cartilage was inserted through an open approach in 18 patients [1]. It has also been used as a columellar strut combined with a porous polyethylene (Medpor) dorsal implant in revision cases [3], to replace extruded alloplastic nasal implants [2], in repair of posttraumatic enophthalmos with a calvarial bone graft [8], and in eardrum reconstruction [9].

A 1991 series of 18 patients with follow-up of 1 to 6 years reported results that were rewarding in most cases, with marked improvement in nasal support [1]. A 1982 review of 62 cases with at least two years of follow-up reported no resorption or immunological response [5][6]. A 2012 series of 32 patients with saddle-nose deformities found over 84% satisfied, with one infection leading to prosthesis removal [3].

The cited series report infection, with one case requiring removal of an implant in the combined-graft series [3]. Surgeons also discuss the general tradeoff that a patient's own cartilage is generally preferred, with donor cartilage used when it is not available [3][4]. Autologous rib harvest carries a minor risk of a pleural tear, which donor tissue avoids [7].

Reports are retrospective case series. They include 18 patients treated with articulated irradiated rib cartilage for nasal reconstruction [1], 32 patients with Medpor plus irradiated cartilage struts [3], a review of 62 cases [5][6], a series on extruded nasal implants [2], an 8-patient enophthalmos series [8] and an eardrum reconstruction chart review [9]. No randomised trials appear in these sources.
